claim: Tumors defective for DNA polymerase (Pol) ε proofreading have the highest tumor mutation burden identified.
source: Tumors defective for DNA polymerase (Pol) ε proofreading have the highest tumor mutation burden identified.
evidence: This is a statement made in the abstract summarizing known findings about Pol ε proofreading-deficient tumors.

claim: Monoallelic Pol ε proofreading deficiency caused a rapid increase in a unique mutation signature when mismatch repair was absent.
source: Absent mismatch repair, monoallelic Pol ε proofreading deficiency caused a rapid increase in a unique mutation signature, similar to that observed in tumors from patients with biallelic mismatch repair deficiency and heterozygous Pol ε mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole genome sequencing and mutation rate measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Restoring mismatch repair was sufficient to suppress the explosive mutation accumulation in Pol ε proofreading-deficient cells.
source: Restoring mismatch repair was sufficient to suppress the explosive mutation accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing mutation rate reduction when Mlh1 was expressed in the cell lines.

claim: Concomitant suppression of mismatch repair is a critical force for driving the explosive mutagenesis seen in tumors expressing exonuclease-deficient Pol ε.
source: These results strongly suggest that concomitant suppression of mismatch repair, a hallmark of colorectal and other aggressive cancers, is a critical force for driving the explosive mutagenesis seen in tumors expressing exonuclease-deficient Pol ε.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing that MMR suppression is required for high mutation rates.

claim: Human cancers share common features of genome instability and mutagenesis.
source: Human cancers share common features of genome instability and mutagenesis (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011) that are the sources of the 103 to 106 somatic mutations observed in the genomes of most types of adult tumors (Stratton, 2011; Wheeler and Wang, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Most adult tumors contain 10^3 to 10^6 somatic mutations.
source: Human cancers share common features of genome instability and mutagenesis (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011) that are the sources of the 103 to 106 somatic mutations observed in the genomes of most types of adult tumors (Stratton, 2011; Wheeler and Wang, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Proofreading defects occur in a wide variety of tumors, with significant enrichment in colorectal and endometrial tumors.
source: Proofreading defects are now known to occur in a wide variety of tumors, with significant enrichment in colorectal and endometrial tumors (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Kandoth et al., 2013; Heitzer and Tomlinson, 2014; Rayner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published tumor sequencing studies.

claim: Mutations in DNA polymerase ε cluster in the exonuclease proofreading domain.
source: Mutations in DNA polymerase (Pol) ε cluster in the exonuclease proofreading domain and the tumors are clinically characterized by several criteria, including being ultrahypermutated, having a unique mutation spectrum, containing a heterozygous Pol ε mutation with no evidence of loss of heterozygosity (LOH) and being microsatellite stable (MSS) (Briggs and Tomlinson, 2013; Church et al., 2013; Palles et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2013; Henninger and Pursell, 2014; Shinbrot et al., 2014; Shlien et al., 2015; Barbari and Shcherbakova, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Pol ε tumors are clinically characterized by being ultrahypermutated, having a unique mutation spectrum, containing a heterozygous Pol ε mutation with no evidence of loss of heterozygosity (LOH) and being microsatellite stable (MSS).
source: Mutations in DNA polymerase (Pol) ε cluster in the exonuclease proofreading domain and the tumors are clinically characterized by several criteria, including being ultrahypermutated, having a unique mutation spectrum, containing a heterozygous Pol ε mutation with no evidence of loss of heterozygosity (LOH) and being microsatellite stable (MSS) (Briggs and Tomlinson, 2013; Church et al., 2013; Palles et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2013; Henninger and Pursell, 2014; Shinbrot et al., 2014; Shlien et al., 2015; Barbari and Shcherbakova, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Pol ε tumors have mutation rates exceeding 100 mutations per megabase.
source: This is the equivalent to what occurs in human tumors with mutations in the Pol ε exonuclease domain and genomic mutation frequencies exceeding 100 mutations per Mb (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Rayner et al., 2016; Shinbrot et al., 2014; Shlien et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published tumor sequencing studies.

claim: Complete, biallelic inactivation of Pol ε proofreading activity causes mutagenesis and carcinogenesis in model organisms.
source: It is clear from studies in model organisms that complete, biallelic inactivation of Pol ε proofreading activity causes mutagenesis and carcinogenesis in model organisms, where mutation rates have been precisely measured using reporter genes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in yeast and mouse models.

claim: Mutation rates are increased in haploid or diploid yeast strains expressing only proofreading-deficient alleles of Pols ε or δ.
source: For example, mutation rates are increased in haploid or diploid yeast strains expressing only proofreading-deficient alleles of Pols ε (Morrison et al., 1991; Morrison and Sugino, 1994; Shcherbakova et al., 2003) or δ (Morrison et al., 1993; Simon et al., 1991; Herr et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published yeast studies.

claim: Mutation rates in proofreading-deficient yeast are further elevated when combined with defects in mismatch repair.
source: These rates are further elevated when combined with defects in mismatch repair, indicating that these errors are made during replication (Morrison and Sugino, 1994; Tran et al., 1999; Tran et al., 1997; Kennedy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published yeast studies.

claim: Homozygous inactivation of both copies of either Pol ε or δ exonuclease activity causes increased mutation rates and cancer in mouse models.
source: In mouse models, homozygous inactivation of both copies of either Pol ε or δ exonuclease activity (Pol εexo-/exo- or Pol δexo-/exo-) causes increased mutation rates and cancer (Albertson et al., 2009; Goldsby et al., 2002; Goldsby et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published mouse studies.

claim: Pol εexo-/exo- mice develop predominantly gastrointestinal tumors while Pol δexo-/exo- mice develop predominantly thymic lymphomas.
source: Interestingly, their tumor spectra are different, with gastrointestinal tumors predominant in Pol εexo-/exo- mice while thymic lymphomas are the major tumor in Pol δexo-/exo- mice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published mouse studies.

claim: Mice with heterozygous inactivation of a single Pol ε proofreading allele fail to develop tumors when mismatch repair is functional.
source: However, mice with a heterozygous inactivation of a single Pol ε proofreading allele (the monoallelic Pol εwt/exo- genotype) fail to develop tumors when mismatch repair is functional (Albertson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published mouse study.

claim: The diploid heterozygous Pol ε exonuclease mutant in yeast is a mutator, but the effect is modest and partially dominant to the wild type allele.
source: The equivalent diploid heterozygous Pol ε exonuclease mutant in yeast is also a mutator, but the effect is modest and partially dominant to the wild type allele and lacks the unique mutation spectrum seen in human tumors (Morrison and Sugino, 1994; Shcherbakova et al., 2003; Morrison et al., 1993; Kane and Shcherbakova, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published yeast studies.

claim: Mismatch repair is responsible for the recognition and removal of replication errors.
source: Mismatch repair is responsible for the recognition and removal of replication errors and deficiencies in this activity cause genome instabilities that can lead to cancer (Kunkel and Erie, 2005; Li, 2008; Jiricny, 2013; Modrich, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on mismatch repair.

claim: Mismatch repair corrects more than 99% of replication errors.
source: Mismatch repair is normally an extremely efficient process, correcting more than 99% of replication errors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mismatch repair efficiency.

claim: MMR efficiencies can vary by over two orders of magnitude and are influenced by multiple factors including strand, polymerase, mismatch nature, sequence context, distance from origin, and replication timing.
source: However, genome-wide studies have recently shown that MMR efficiencies can vary by over two orders of magnitude and are influenced by a number of factors, including the strand on which the mismatch occurs, the polymerase that made the error, the nature of the mismatch, local sequence context, distance from the origin and replication timing (Hawk et al., 2005; Hombauer et al., 2011; Lujan et al., 2014; Lujan et al., 2012; Supek and Lehner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published genome-wide studies.

claim: Patients with biallelic mismatch repair disorder (bMMRD) have biallelic germline inactivating mutations in a mismatch repair gene and develop early-onset tumors with microsatellite instability.
source: Patients with biallelic mismatch repair disorder (bMMRD) have biallelic germline inactivating mutations in a mismatch repair gene and are completely lacking mismatch repair and develop a number of early-onset tumors in which microsatellite instability (MSI) is readily detectable (Durno et al., 2017; Wimmer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published clinical studies.

claim: A subset of bMMRD patients acquires a later somatic mutation in a single allele of Pol ε, leading to very aggressive tumor development.
source: A subset of these patients acquires a later somatic mutation in a single allele of Pol ε, leading to very aggressive tumor development.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published clinical studies.

claim: Mutation rates from Pol εwt/exo- MMR−/− tumors have been estimated on the order of several hundred per genome duplication.
source: Mutation rates from these Pol εwt/exo- MMR−/− tumors have been estimated on the order of several hundred per genome duplication (Shlien et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Mice with heterozygous Pol εwt/exo- combined with homozygous MMR−/− develop tumors within 1–2 months.
source: This is consistent with results from model systems as mice with the equivalent genotype (heterozygous Pol εwt/exo- combined with homozygous MMR−/−) develop tumors within 1–2 months (Treuting et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published mouse study.

claim: Yeast strains with heterozygous Pol ε exonuclease deficiency combined with MMR deficiency are strong mutators.
source: The equivalent yeast strains are strong mutators as well (Shcherbakova et al., 2003; Morrison et al., 1993; Kennedy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published yeast studies.

claim: Sporadic POLE tumors are generally microsatellite stable.
source: However, since sporadic POLE tumors are generally microsatellite stable, the role of MMR in Pol ε proofreading-deficiency in the development of these MSS tumors remains a critical unanswered question.
evidence: This is established knowledge about POLE tumors from published studies.

claim: rAAV-mediated gene targeting was used to engineer a diploid human cell line to express one allele of Pol ε with the D275A/E277A double substitution.
source: To test whether inactivation of a single allele of Pol ε proofreading was sufficient to cause a mutator phenotype in human cells, we used recombinant adenoassociated virus (rAAV)-mediated gene targeting to engineer a diploid human cell line to express one allele of Pol ε with the D275A/E277A double substitution (Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and figures showing the gene targeting strategy.

claim: The D275A/E277A mutation inactivates exonuclease proofreading in vitro.
source: We chose the D275A/E277A mutation because it inactivates exonuclease proofreading in vitro (Shcherbakova et al., 2003; Korona et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published biochemical studies.

claim: The parental cell line, HCT-116, is constitutively mismatch repair-deficient due to an inactivating mutation in Mlh1.
source: The parental cell line, HCT-116, is constitutively mismatch repair-deficient due to an inactivating mutation in Mlh1, thus allowing us to first define the contributions of proofreading deficiency separately to mutagenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the HCT-116 cell line.

claim: A moderate mutator effect was seen in Pol εwt/exo- heterozygotes.
source: A moderate mutator effect was seen in Pol εwt/exo- heterozygotes (Figure 1A), indicating the exo- allele was partially dominant over the endogenous exo + allele, similar to what is seen in a mismatch repair-deficient diploid cell line heterozygous for a Pol ε proofreading mutation, pol2-4/+pms1/pms1 (Pavlov et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The exo- allele was partially dominant over the endogenous exo+ allele.
source: A moderate mutator effect was seen in Pol εwt/exo- heterozygotes (Figure 1A), indicating the exo- allele was partially dominant over the endogenous exo + allele, similar to what is seen in a mismatch repair-deficient diploid cell line heterozygous for a Pol ε proofreading mutation, pol2-4/+pms1/pms1 (Pavlov et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference from the mutation rate data and comparison to published yeast studies.

claim: The increase in mutation rate in Pol εwt/exo- mismatch repair-deficient cells was primarily due to base pair substitutions.
source: The increase in mutation rate seen in the Pol εwt/exo- mismatch repair-deficient cells was primarily due to base pair substitutions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Frameshift error rates did not change in Pol εwt/exo- cells.
source: Frameshift error rates did not change, in agreement with previous findings in vitro that Pol ε proofreading primarily strongly corrects base-base mispairs with little effect on frameshift fidelity (Korona et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to published in vitro studies.

claim: The D275A/E277A mutant made TCT→TAT transversions at a significantly higher rate in vitro than the wild type exonuclease-proficient Pol ε enzyme.
source: Using an in vitro lacZ reversion substrate that specifically measures TCT→TAT transversions (Shinbrot et al., 2014; Shlien et al., 2015), the D275A/E277A mutant made these errors at a significantly higher rate in vitro than the wild type exonuclease-proficient Pol ε enzyme (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The elevated TCT→TAT error rate observed with the D275A/E277A mutant was not statistically different from those measured with the S459F and S461P Pol ε cancer mutants.
source: Importantly, the elevated TCT→TAT error rate we observed with the D275A/E277A mutant was not statistically different from those measured with the S459F and S461P Pol ε cancer mutants previously (Shinbrot et al., 2014; Shlien et al., 2015), suggesting a common mechanism of mutagenesis for these hotspot mutations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and comparison to published studies.

claim: Based on the measured mutation rate for HPRT1 in Pol εwt/exo- cells lacking mismatch repair, a μBS value of 0.23 × 10−7 mutations per base pair per genome duplication was calculated.
source: Based on our measured mutation rate for HPRT1 (μL) in Pol εwt/exo- cells lacking mismatch repair (180 × 10−7), we calculated a μBS value of 0.23 × 10−7 mutations per base pair per genome duplication.
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental mutation rate data.

claim: Whole-genome sequencing revealed 5,282 SNVs unique to the P14 population after 14 population doublings.
source: Whole-genome sequencing revealed 5,282 SNVs unique to the P14 population, 5.8-fold higher than that predicted from the μL at HPRT1.
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: The number of mutations observed genome-wide was 5.8-fold higher than predicted from the HPRT1 mutation rate.
source: Whole-genome sequencing revealed 5,282 SNVs unique to the P14 population, 5.8-fold higher than that predicted from the μL at HPRT1.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data from WGS and HPRT1 mutation rates.

claim: Mutations observed in HPRT1 may slightly underrepresent those found genome-wide.
source: Mutations observed in HPRT1 in this cell line may thus slightly underrepresent those found genome-wide.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of HPRT1 and genome-wide mutation rates.

claim: Reporter gene mutation rates are consistently 6–8-fold lower than concurrently measured whole-genome mutation rates in microbes.
source: This difference is consistent with what is seen in microbes, where reporter gene mutation rates are consistently 6–8-fold lower than concurrently measured whole-genome mutation rates, likely due to phenotypic lag, strong selective pressure and transcription in the reporter gene (Drake, 2012; Jee et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published microbial studies.

claim: C→A transversions exceeding 20% of all base pair substitutions is a primary characteristic of mutation spectra from tumors containing Pol ε exonuclease domain mutations.
source: C→A transversions exceeding 20% of all base pair substitutions is a primary characteristic of mutation spectra from tumors containing Pol ε exonuclease domain mutations (Rayner et al., 2016; Shinbrot et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published tumor sequencing studies.

claim: C→A transversions were increased significantly in the Pol εwt/exo- cells as compared to the control Pol εwt/wt spectrum, accounting for 46% of all base pair substitutions.
source: C→A transversions were increased significantly in the Pol εwt/exo- cells as compared to the control Pol εwt/wt spectrum, accounting for 46% of all base pair substitutions (Figure 2A, χ2 = 11.874, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Whole exome sequencing from HCT-116 cells from two independent studies showed roughly 10% C→A transversions.
source: These were not cell line artifacts, as whole exome sequencing from HCT-116 cells from two independent studies ([Abaan et al., 2013] and this study) showed roughly 10% C→A transversions (Figure 2A, p>0.5).
evidence: This is supported by whole exome sequencing data from this study and a published study.

claim: HCC2998 cells, which harbor the Pol εwt/P286R mutation, showed a significant increase in C→A transversions relative to Pol εwt/wt cells.
source: HCC2998 cells, which harbor the Pol εwt/P286R mutation, also showed a significant increase in C→A transversions relative to Pol εwt/wt cells (Figure 2A, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by data extracted from a published study and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Two sequence context mutational hotspots were observed: C→A transversions in TCT context and T→G transversions in TTT context.
source: Two sequence context mutational hotspots were observed that are consistent with Pol ε exonuclease domain mutant spectra: C→A transversions in TCT context and T→G transversions in TTT context and, to a lesser extent, ATT and GTT contexts (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: These hotspots are seen in Pol ε tumors from patients with bMMRD.
source: These hotspots are seen in Pol ε tumors from patients with bMMRD (Shlien et al., 2015), colorectal and endometrial cancer (Alexandrov and Stratton, 2014; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Kandoth et al., 2013; Shinbrot et al., 2014), as well as in the Pol ε-P286R HCC2998 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, data extracted from [Abaan et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published tumor sequencing studies and data from HCC2998 cells.

claim: TCT and TTT context mutations are not mutational hotspots in HCT-116 cells with wild type Pol ε.
source: These are not mutational hotspots in HCT-116 cells, which contain wild type Pol ε (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by whole exome sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The largest number of mutations that arose during the 14 doublings were C→A transversions in triplet contexts containing adjacent cytosines: CCA, CCT, CCC and CCG.
source: The largest number of mutations that arose during the 14 doublings were C→A transversions in triplet contexts containing adjacent cytosines: CCA, CCT, CCC and CCG.
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: The increase in C→A mutations in the CCT context was also seen in Pol ε exonuclease domain (EDM) tumors from bMMRD patients.
source: The increase in C→A mutations in the CCT context was also seen in Pol ε exonuclease domain (EDM) tumors from bMMRD patients (Shlien et al., 2015), suggesting a link between Pol ε replication errors left uncorrected by mismatch repair.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study and suggests a mechanistic link.

claim: C→A mutations in CCA, CCC and CCG contexts are slightly elevated in Mutation Signature 20, which has been associated with loss of mismatch repair.
source: C→A mutations in CCA, CCC and CCG contexts are slightly elevated in Mutation Signature 20, which has been associated with loss of mismatch repair (Alexandrov et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published mutation signature study.

claim: The lack of C→T transitions in TCG contexts is significantly different from colorectal and endometrial Pol ε tumors, but consistent with their absence from bMMRD tumors with Pol ε EDM mutations.
source: The lack of C→T transitions in TCG contexts is significantly different from colorectal and endometrial Pol ε tumors, but consistent with their absence from bMMRD tumors with Pol ε EDM mutations (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Kandoth et al., 2013; Shinbrot et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data to published tumor sequencing studies.

claim: Lentiviral Mlh1 expression reduced mutation rates at the HPRT1 locus by 14- to 20-fold in the wild type polymerase background.
source: Lentiviral Mlh1 expression reduced mutation rates at the HPRT1 locus by 14- to 20-fold in the wild type polymerase background (Figure 3B), similar to the 12-fold reduction reported when the Mlh1-encoding chromosome 3 was added back to HCT-116 cells ([Glaab and Tindall, 1997; Tindall et al., 1998]; 73 × 10−7 and 5.9 × 10−7; 12.4-fold reduction), indicating that the expressed Mlh1 is functional.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and comparison to published studies.

claim: Mlh1 expression in Pol εwt/exo- cells caused an over 50-fold decrease in the mutation rate.
source: Mlh1 expression in Pol εwt/exo- cells caused an over 50-fold decrease in the mutation rate (to 2.3 and 3.0 × 10−7, Figure 3B), making them indistinguishable from those measured in Pol εwt/wt cells with Mlh1 expressed (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Msh3 is unlikely to play a significant role in correcting the exonuclease-deficient Pol ε errors since HCT-116 cells are deficient in this factor and it was not added back in these experiments.
source: This result also suggests that Msh3 is unlikely to play a significant role in correcting the exonuclease-deficient Pol ε errors since HCT-116 cells are deficient in this factor and it was not added back in these experiments (Papadopoulos et al., 1994).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results and citation to a published study about HCT-116 cells.

claim: Whole exome sequencing showed similar low mutation rates in Pol εwt/wt and Pol εwt/exo- cells with mismatch repair (13 × 10−9 Mut/bp/doubling and 18 × 10−9 Mut/bp/doubling, respectively).
source: Using the PDL = 0 samples as matched normal controls, we measured similar low mutation rates in Pol εwt/wt and Pol εwt/exo- cells (13 × 10−9 Mut/bp/doubling and 18 × 10−9 Mut/bp/doubling, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by whole exome sequencing data.

claim: There was a statistically significant increase in C→A transversions between the mismatch repair-proficient Pol εwt/exo- cells and the mismatch repair-proficient Pol εwt/wt cells.
source: Interestingly, there was a statistically significant increase in C→A transversions (p=0.0002) between the mismatch repair-proficient Pol εwt/exo- cells and the mismatch repair-proficient Pol εwt/wt cells, while no statistically significant difference was found in any other class of base pair substitution (p>0.2 for each of the six classes, Fisher's Exact Test).
evidence: This is supported by whole exome sequencing data and statistical analysis.

claim: The majority of replication errors made by the Pol ε-D275A/E277A mutant are corrected by mismatch repair.
source: These results indicate that the majority of replication errors made by the Pol ε-D275A/E277A mutant are in fact corrected by mismatch repair.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing suppression of mutation rates by MMR.

claim: Large and rapid mutation accumulation occurs when Pol ε exonuclease domain mutations occur along with inactivation of mismatch repair.
source: We show that large and rapid mutation accumulation occurs when Pol ε exonuclease domain mutations occur along with inactivation of mismatch repair.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from whole genome sequencing.

claim: Most mutations in Pol ε exonuclease-deficient MMR-deficient cells are specific transversion mutations known to be hotspots of exonuclease-deficient Pol ε mutagenesis.
source: Most of these are specific transversion mutations known to be hotspots of exonuclease-deficient Pol ε mutagenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from whole genome sequencing showing specific mutation patterns.

claim: The large increase in mutation rate in Pol ε exonuclease-deficient cells is largely suppressed by functional mismatch repair.
source: We further show that this large increase in mutation rate is largely suppressed by functional mismatch repair.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing mutation rate reduction with MMR expression.

claim: The mechanism of replication error mutagenesis in sporadic tumors with heterozygous Pol ε mutations likely requires an additional feature beyond simple heterozygous loss of proofreading.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the mechanism of replication error mutagenesis in sporadic tumors with heterozygous Pol ε mutations likely requires an additional feature, several of which are described below, including suppression of MMR and alternative effects on Pol ε activity.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results and discussion of possible mechanisms.

claim: The D275A/E277A double amino acid substitution has been shown to inactivate exonuclease proofreading in vitro and cause increased reporter gene mutation rates in yeast and mammalian cells.
source: This double amino acid substitution has been shown to inactivate exonuclease proofreading in vitro and cause increased reporter gene mutation rates in yeast and mammalian cells (Morrison et al., 1991; Morrison and Sugino, 1994; Tran et al., 1999; Albertson et al., 2009; Korona et al., 2011; Shcherbakova and Pavlov, 1996; Agbor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Unbiased whole-genome sequencing confirmed the rapid accumulation of Pol ε-specific mutations seen in POLE tumors lacking functional mismatch repair.
source: Unbiased whole-genome sequencing confirmed the rapid accumulation of Pol ε-specific mutations seen in POLE tumors lacking functional mismatch repair (Shlien et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental whole genome sequencing data and citation to a published study.

claim: The total number of measured SNVs suggests a mutation rate of 380 mutations per population doubling.
source: The total number of measured SNVs suggests a mutation rate of 380 mutations per population doubling, similar to the 608 mutations per cell cycle calculated for a mismatch repair-deficient brain tumor harboring a Pol ε exonuclease domain mutation.
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental whole genome sequencing data.

claim: The cellular mutation rate values possibly underestimate the true Pol ε exonuclease-deficient mutation rate for several reasons.
source: Our cellular mutation rate values possibly underestimate the true Pol ε exonuclease-deficient mutation rate for several reasons.
evidence: This is speculation based on discussion of potential limitations.

claim: The data were generated from a cancer cell line with a large number of pre-existing mutations.
source: Our data were generated from a cancer cell line with a large number of pre-existing mutations (Abaan et al., 2013), as well as additional mutations that have assuredly arisen during passaging in the laboratory.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study characterizing HCT-116 cells.

claim: No additional mutations in POLE were sequenced, suggesting that viability of this cell line is not due to an acquired mutation elsewhere in POLE acting to suppress the mutation rate.
source: Importantly, no additional mutations in POLE were sequenced, suggesting that viability of this cell line is not due to an acquired mutation elsewhere in POLE acting to suppress the mutation rate, as occurs frequently in yeast (Herr et al., 2011a; Williams et al., 2013; Herr et al., 2011b; Dennis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data and citations to published yeast studies.

claim: Mutations that arise in the last several rounds of replication and those that fall below 5% allele frequency would not meet the threshold for scoring as a true SNV.
source: An additional reason that our mutation rates may underestimate the true mutation rate is that mutations that arise in the last several rounds of replication and those that fall below 5% allele frequency would not meet the threshold for scoring as a true SNV.
evidence: This is speculation about technical limitations of the sequencing approach.

claim: The per base pair mutation rates in heterozygous diploid human cells are similar to those in haploid yeast with complete Pol ε exonuclease deficiency and disrupted MMR.
source: These rates are also similar to the per base pair mutation rates in haploid yeast with complete Pol ε exonuclease deficiency and disrupted MMR (Kennedy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data to published yeast studies.

claim: Individual cell mutation rates in yeast could vary by an order of magnitude.
source: A key finding from the yeast study was that individual cell mutation rates could vary by an order of magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published yeast study.

claim: The unique mutation spectrum seen in POLE tumors was recapitulated in the gene-targeted cell lines, with one notable exception.
source: The unique mutation spectrum seen in POLE tumors was recapitulated in our gene-targeted cell lines, with one notable exception.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data to published tumor mutation spectra.

claim: Many C→A transversions occur in a highly specific triplet sequence context, TCT, in tumors.
source: In tumors, many C→A transversions occur in a highly specific triplet sequence context, TCT, which we also see in the cell lines, though not to the same proportion as in the tumor genomes.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data to published tumor mutation spectra.

claim: Increased T→G transversions in TTT context are observed, similar to Pol ε tumors.
source: We also observe increased T→G transversions in TTT (and to a lesser extent ATT and CTT) context, similar to Pol ε tumors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and comparison to published tumor mutation spectra.

claim: The TCT→TAT mutation is enriched in yeast with the P286R equivalent allele.
source: Interestingly, this particular mutation is also enriched in yeast with the P286R equivalent allele (Barbari and Shcherbakova, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published yeast study.

claim: There is a lack of TCG→TTG transitions in the dataset.
source: What is notable, however, is the lack of TCG→TTG transitions in our dataset.
evidence: This is supported by experimental whole genome sequencing data.

claim: TCG→TTG transitions are the second most frequent Pol ε-specific mutation in the TCGA database.
source: This is the second most frequent Pol ε-specific mutation in the TCGA database.
evidence: This is supported by knowledge from published TCGA studies.

claim: TCG→TTG transitions were not found elevated in the Pol ε bMMRD brain tumor mutation spectrum.
source: TCG→TTG transitions were also not found elevated in the Pol ε bMMRD brain tumor mutation spectrum.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: The difference in TCG→TTG transitions may reflect tissue differences.
source: This difference may reflect interesting, but as-yet undefined tissue differences.
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for observed differences.

claim: The Pol ε mutants found in tumors may be intrinsically different biochemically from the double alanine substitution mutant.
source: Another possible explanation for these differences is that the Pol ε mutants found in tumors are somehow intrinsically different biochemically from the double alanine substitution mutant used in the current study.
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for observed differences.

claim: The monoallelic Pol ε-P286R mutant is a 2.3- to 12-fold stronger mutator than the pol2-4 mutant when measured in a diploid yeast strain.
source: Depending on the reporter gene used, the monoallelic Pol ε-P286R mutant is a 2.3- to 12-fold stronger mutator than the pol2-4 mutant (equivalent to the human Pol ε D275A/E277A studied here) when measured in a diploid yeast strain (Kane and Shcherbakova, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published yeast study.

claim: Direct biochemical comparisons of activity and fidelity between several cancer mutant constructs and the D275A/E277A construct have not shown any significant differences.
source: However, a number of direct biochemical comparisons of activity and fidelity (Figure 1C, (Shinbrot et al., 2014; Shlien et al., 2015) and unpublished observations) between several cancer mutant constructs and the D275A/E277A construct have not yet shown any significant differences that could account for this.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to published studies.

claim: Certain DNA Pol mutants can cause increased mutagenesis by inducing expansions of normal dNTP pools in yeast and human cells.
source: Certain DNA Pol mutants, including some found in human tumors, can cause increased mutagenesis by inducing expansions of normal dNTP pools in yeast and human cells (Dennis et al., 2017; Mertz et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The pol2-4 allele has no effect on dNTP pools in yeast.
source: Interestingly, the pol2-4 allele has no effect on dNTP pools in yeast, suggesting a possible explanation for possible allelic differences with functional MMR.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published yeast studies and is used to infer possible mechanisms.

claim: In heterozygous Pol εwt/exo- cells with functional mismatch repair, mutation rates were suppressed to the levels seen in cells with wild type Pol ε.
source: In heterozygous Pol εwt/exo- cells with functional mismatch repair, mutation rates were suppressed to the levels seen in cells with wild type Pol ε.
evidence: This is supported by experimental mutation rate data.

claim: Mutation rates in MMR-proficient Pol εwt/exo- cells would be insufficient to give rise to ultrahypermutated tumors in a matter of months.
source: These rates would be insufficient to give rise to ultrahypermutated tumors in a matter of months.
evidence: This is an inference from the measured mutation rates.

claim: There is no explosive accumulation of triplet context-specific mutations in the MMR-proficient Pol εwt/exo- cells.
source: In addition, there is no explosive accumulation of triplet context-specific mutations in the MMR-proficient Pol εwt/exo- cells that is seen in these tumors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental whole exome sequencing data.

claim: Simple heterozygous loss of two Pol ε exonuclease metal chelating residues on a single allele of POLE is insufficient to drive Pol ε ultramutational specificity.
source: Our results support a model in which simple heterozygous loss of two Pol ε exonuclease metal chelating residues on a single allele of POLE is insufficient to drive Pol ε ultramutational specificity.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: Additional factors are likely required to help drive the ultramutated phenotype observed in POLE tumors, including suppression of mismatch repair.
source: Additional factors are likely required to help drive the ultramutated phenotype observed in POLE tumors, including suppression of mismatch repair, discussed below.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results and discussion.

claim: In bMMRD, the complete lack of mismatch repair prior to Pol ε mutation leads to the moderate accumulation of Pol ε-independent replication errors.
source: In bMMRD, the complete lack of mismatch repair prior to Pol ε mutation leads to the moderate accumulation of Pol ε-independent replication errors (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference from the model shown in Figure 5 and published studies.

claim: Mutation rates increase dramatically upon loss of proofreading in one allele in bMMRD patients.
source: Mutation rates then increase dramatically upon loss of proofreading in one allele, with the Pol ε error signature representing a smaller fraction of the total errors, which is seen in these tumors (Shlien et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Pol ε mutations in somatic tumors can occur first and early, but later suppression of MMR would then accelerate overall mutation rates.
source: Our results suggest that Pol ε mutations in somatic tumors can occur first and early, but later suppression of MMR would then accelerate overall mutation rates to that seen in the ultramutated tumors, while the signature mutation proportion remains high (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Kandoth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results and comparison to published tumor data.

claim: 85% (22/26) of the TCGA Pol ε tumors have a mutation in at least one mismatch repair gene.
source: 85% (22/26) of the TCGA Pol ε tumors also have a mutation in at least one mismatch repair gene, most of which (18/22) harbor at least one nonsense mutation, which are more likely to be inactivating mutations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most TCGA Pol ε tumors with MMR gene mutations (18/22) harbor at least one nonsense mutation.
source: 85% (22/26) of the TCGA Pol ε tumors also have a mutation in at least one mismatch repair gene, most of which (18/22) harbor at least one nonsense mutation, which are more likely to be inactivating mutations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several POLE tumors were initially classified as MSI in the original TCGA studies.
source: In the original TCGA studies, several POLE tumors were actually first classified as MSI (three as MSI-H; five as MSI-L) (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Kandoth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published TCGA studies.

claim: Analysis of sequencing reads from 46 homonucleotide runs in the POLE endometrial tumors showed no evidence of instability.
source: Analysis of sequencing reads from 46 homonucleotide runs in the POLE endometrial tumors showed no evidence of instability, so the POLE tumors were then reclassified as MSS (Shinbrot et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: A subset of POLE tumors may have a microsatellite instability defect at repeats more complex than homonucleotides.
source: However, the initial TCGA studies used both homo- and di-nucleotide loci to score MSI, raising the possibility that a subset of POLE tumors have a microsatellite instability defect at repeats more complex than homonucleotides.
evidence: This is speculation based on the methods used in TCGA studies.

claim: The repeat unit size, the number of repeats and the repeat sequence composition have very strong influences on the variability of microsatellite mutagenesis.
source: Indeed, the repeat unit size, the number of repeats and the repeat sequence composition are known to have very strong influences on the variability of microsatellite mutagenesis (Shah et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Most (15/18) of the MMR gene nonsense mutations in POLE tumors are the result of TCT→TAT transversions.
source: Curiously, however, most (15/18) of the MMR gene nonsense mutations are the result of TCT→TAT transversions, raising the possibility that Pol ε mutation occurs first and possibly even promotes subsequent mutational inactivation of MMR.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA data and suggests a possible mechanism.

claim: 15% (4/26) of Pol ε mutant colorectal and endometrial tumors lacked a mutation in any mismatch repair gene and showed no evidence of MLH1 promoter hypermethylation.
source: Of all the Pol ε mutant colorectal and endometrial tumors sequenced in the TCGA studies, 15% (4/26) lacked a mutation in any mismatch repair gene and also showed no evidence of MLH1 promoter hypermethylation, demonstrating that the ultramutated phenotype can arise when mismatch repair is intact at both the genetic and epigenetic level.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA data.

claim: Mismatch repair activity may be suppressed at some point during POLE tumor development.
source: An alternative possibility is that mismatch repair activity is suppressed at some point during POLE tumor development.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: A number of conditions have been shown to transiently and reversibly lower mismatch repair protein levels and inhibit mismatch repair activity.
source: A number of conditions have been shown to transiently and reversibly lower mismatch repair protein levels and inhibit mismatch repair activity, including hypoxia, oxidative damage, inflammation, reduced pH, exposure to adriamycin or cadmium and treatment with mutagenic dNTP analogs (Banerjee and Flores-Rozas, 2005; Francia et al., 2005; Larson and Drummond, 2001; Mihaylova et al., 2003; Chang et al., 2002; Hile et al., 2013; Iwaizumi et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2014; Negishi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Transient mismatch repair suppression has been seen in the context of proofreading-deficiency in E. coli.
source: Perhaps even more intriguingly, transient mismatch repair suppression has been seen in the context of proofreading-deficiency in E. coli (Fijalkowska and Schaaper, 1996; Schaaper and Radman, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published bacterial studies.

claim: Replication errors made by the proofreading-deficient allele tested were insufficient to suppress MMR.
source: While replication errors made by the proofreading-deficient allele tested here were clearly insufficient to suppress MMR, it is possible that the nature and rate of errors made by cancer-associated alleles might be sufficient to saturate and overwhelm MMR pathways.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results and speculation about other alleles.

claim: Loss of a single Pol ε proofreading allele is sufficient to drive a subset of the observed clinical characteristics of Pol ε tumors, provided mismatch repair is compromised.
source: Our results support the idea that loss of a single Pol ε proofreading allele is sufficient to drive a subset of the observed clinical characteristics of Pol ε tumors, provided mismatch repair is compromised in some way.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: In the presence of fully functional MMR the appearance of the ultrahypermutated mutation signature may be more directly related to some as yet uncharacterized additional defect in the mutant polymerase.
source: These observations further support the idea that in the presence of fully functional MMR the appearance of the ultrahypermutated mutation signature may be more directly related to some as yet uncharacterized additional defect in the mutant polymerase (Barbari and Shcherbakova, 2017).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to a published study.
